comment: The principle states that countries 'should not be dependent on actors outside their jurisdiction for the continued operation or evolution of their core digital health infrastructure'. Artificial intelligence introduces a form of cross-jurisdictional dependency that the guidance does not name. A country may own every registry, exchange layer and record described in this architecture and still have every clinical decision-support inference executed on a model hosted in another jurisdiction, under that jurisdiction's export controls, and subject to a supplier's unilateral pricing and deprecation decisions. That is the dependency this principle forbids, arriving through a door the architecture leaves undescribed. The distinction that matters architecturally is not whether AI is used but whether the model can be executed within the country's own infrastructure.

public.suggestedRevision: Extend the Autonomy and Sovereignty principle with a sentence to the effect: 'Where artificial intelligence forms part of a health capability, the architecture should preserve the option of in-jurisdiction inference — that is, models whose weights can be hosted and operated on national infrastructure. Dependence on a remotely hosted model that cannot be substituted or relocated is a sovereignty risk of the same class as dependence on a foreign-operated registry, and should be assessed as such.'
